measurement.happened:
The dominant story of the week in Iran was the accelerating tension between a fragile truce and the very real prospect of renewed US military strikes, all set against the backdrop of the US midterm elections scheduled for November 3. Multiple headlines confirm that the US launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets, including fishing boats off Qeshm Island, while Iran shot down a US drone over Bandar Abbas and targeted US air defenses, aircraft, and buildings at Middle East bases (Reuters, AP, DW, Al Jazeera). Iran's Supreme Leader Khamenei warned that any retaliation would have no 'geographic limits,' and the president Pezeshkian said it was time to end the war from a 'position of strength' (AP, DW, Bloomberg). Trump oscillated between saying the war was 'going to get wrapped up soon' and threatening to hit 'one or two sites,' while also telling allies to prepare for a possible short, intense renewal of fighting after the midterms (Reuters, TV5Monde, WSJ, CNBC). The Pentagon's war cost was pegged at $47.1 billion, and Defense Secretary Hegseth fired the Pentagon's top military planner, a move widely read as a signal that operational plans for a new phase were being finalized (AP, CNN, CNBC, WSJ).

The second major theme was the sharp escalation of maritime attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's IRGC Navy reported four tankers catching fire after striking mines, and the Financial Times described this as an 'apparent tactical shift' toward limpet mines rather than larger weapons. Oil spills from the tanker attacks washed up on UAE beaches, a Pakistan LNG cargo was attacked with Iranian approval, and Iran threatened legal action against South Korean Sinokor vessels. Somali piracy also resurfaced as shipping routes were rattled. Despite the attacks, tankers continued to push through, and oil prices settled at six-month highs before easing slightly on diplomatic hopes (Reuters, AP, FT, Bloomberg, CNBC, CNN, DW).

The third theme was an intense wave of diplomacy. Qatari mediators made repeated trips to Tehran in what was described as a 'last-ditch' effort to revive a ceasefire deal. The so-called 'Mecca Pact' brought Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani officials together in Tehran, where Pezeshkian called for 'regional unity' and Iran reported 'very good' discussions. Vice President Vance reached out to Iranian hardliners to offer medical supplies as a goodwill gesture, and Iran's foreign minister called the US outreach a 'positive step.' Pakistan's military was 'cautiously optimistic.' Yet Iran simultaneously told mediators it saw only 'unacceptable ideas' in the latest proposals, and Qatar said Iran needed to show good intentions. The overall picture was one of genuine but fragile back-channel activity, with no breakthrough yet (Reuters, CNN, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, CNBC, FT).

The fourth theme was the economic shock spreading globally. US taxpayers were on the hook for $47 billion. Oil jumped to six-month highs, European gas broke above 100 euros, Canada raised interest rates to contain the oil spike, Japan scaled back fuel subsidies, and ANZ raised its oil price forecast. In Iran itself, the fuel crisis deepened, natural gas ran short, and ordinary Iranians cut back on essentials. Companies from Unilever to brewers to airlines to Kia reported rising costs, while US oil majors like Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs. The UK tried to give households 'breathing space' on energy prices (Reuters, AP, AFP, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, DW).

The fifth theme was Israel's election and its impact on the Iran question. Netanyahu, campaigning with Trump's endorsement, suggested a restart of the war with Iran, while his challenger Eisenkot urged unity and accused Netanyahu of playing a 'dangerous game' with Tehran. Analysts noted that a Netanyahu defeat would make the Iran war harder for the US to pursue, and the caretaker government question left the door open to an Iran attack either way (Reuters, AP, TV5Monde, FT, DW, CNBC).

The sixth theme was the nuclear question. The IAEA reported that Iran had not tried to repair the nuclear facilities damaged in earlier US strikes. Meanwhile, Iranian lawmakers called for withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty, signaling growing domestic hardening on the nuclear issue (AP, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera).

The seventh theme was espionage and intelligence activity. Two men were charged in the UK over the alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford, an airbase used for US strikes on Iran. An overseas handler linked to Iran was identified as behind the foiled attack. Russian satellites were reported to have helped Iran's allies strike Saudi Arabia. Iran's hidden network of military agencies was found to be slipping hardware past the US blockade, and sanctioned jet fuel purchases were disguised through Myanmar. US intelligence warned that Iran was trying harder to target American personnel in the Middle East (Reuters, BBC, CNN, DW, WSJ, AP).

The eighth theme was domestic politics and society in Iran. The Revolutionary Court sentenced acclaimed film director Jafar Panahi to a new prison term and travel ban after his return home. The security chief met with Supreme Leader Khamenei after the Mecca Pact talks. Tehran was rushing to rebuild during the fragile truce. One man whose twelve family members were killed in the war told Al Jazeera, 'My life is buried here.' The war was visibly reshaping daily life, with energy shortages, currency pressure, and a sense of national endurance (Reuters, AP, DW, FT, Al Jazeera).

The ninth theme was regional spillover. Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia multiple times before and during the Tehran talks. Saudi Arabia intercepted missiles and drones. Hezbollah was reported to be preparing for a new regional war with funds from Iran. Egypt's foreign minister warned that an escalation would be 'more destructive.' The broader Gulf was on edge, with American embassies tightening security and the US warning Gulf states to prepare for possible strikes (Reuters, AP, CNN, AFP, CNBC, Al Jazeera).
measurement.expected:
Theme 1: Diplomacy in the final stretch before and just after the US midterms. Confidence: probable. Qatari mediators are already in Tehran, Vance has opened a channel, and the Mecca Pact delegation has met Pezeshkian. The political logic for both sides is to either lock in a deal before November 3 or to wait until the new US Congress is seated. I expect at least one more round of high-level talks in the week of November 1-8, likely in Doha or Tehran. However, Iran's public statements that the proposals contain 'unacceptable ideas' and Khamenei's reiterated conditions suggest that a full agreement is not guaranteed. A limited framework or a renewed ceasefire with verification language is the most likely diplomatic outcome. A complete deal is possible but I would not call it probable.

Theme 2: Limited US strikes or a 'show of force.' Confidence: probable. Trump has threatened to hit 'one or two sites,' the Pentagon has reorganized its planning staff, and the USS George Washington has been rearming. The most likely scenario is not a full-scale war but a calibrated strike on one or two targets (possibly a missile site, a naval asset, or a nuclear-related facility) timed either just before or just after the midterms to frame the political narrative. Iran's warning of 'unfettered retaliation' and its targeting of US bases suggest it is preparing for exactly this. I would put the probability of at least one significant US strike in the next seven days at roughly 55-65 percent. A full-scale 'finish it off' campaign is less likely (maybe 20-25 percent) because the political cost to Trump in a divided Congress is high.

Theme 3: Continued Hormuz disruption. Confidence: almost certain. The shift to limpet mines and the four-tanker incident show Iran is willing to raise the maritime stakes without a full naval confrontation. I expect at least one or two more tanker incidents or mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz in the coming week, particularly if diplomacy stalls. The tactical logic is to keep oil prices elevated and pressure Gulf states to push harder for a deal. Full closure of the strait is unlikely, but a 10-20 percent increase in insurance premiums and a visible uptick in tanker insurance costs is almost certain.

Theme 4: Oil and energy markets stay elevated. Confidence: almost certain. With gas above 100 euros, oil at six-month highs, and the US war cost at $47 billion, the market is pricing in continued uncertainty. I expect Brent to trade in the mid-to-upper 70s or low 80s dollar range, with periodic spikes on headline risk. European gas will likely stay above 90-100 euros. The US dollar will be under pressure from the war spending. Iranian fuel shortages at home will continue, with possible rationing or blackouts in the north during the first cold snaps of November.

Theme 5: Post-election Israel and the Iran question. Confidence: probable that the Israeli election result (likely held around November 2-3, 2026) will be a visible factor in the next week's Iran headlines. If Netanyahu wins, expect him to push for a more aggressive posture toward Iran and to coordinate with the US on next steps. If Eisenkot or a coalition partner wins, expect a more cautious, diplomacy-first approach. Either way, the caretaker government period will create a window of uncertainty that both Washington and Tehran will watch carefully.

Theme 6: Nuclear signals. Confidence: possible. The IAEA finding that Iran has not repaired bombed nuclear sites, combined with lawmakers calling for NPT withdrawal, suggests Iran is keeping its nuclear option warm. I would not expect a formal NPT withdrawal vote in the next week, but I do expect at least one parliamentary or media statement reinforcing the message. A snap IAEA inspection or a UN Security Council discussion is possible but not probable.

Theme 7: Espionage and covert activity. Confidence: probable that the RAF Fairford case will generate at least one more court hearing or media development in the UK. The broader pattern of Iranian intelligence activity in the region (targeting US personnel, satellite-assisted Houthi strikes, disguised fuel purchases) will continue. I would not expect a major new espionage scandal in Iran itself in the next week, but the 'espionage threats blur lines between security and dissent' dynamic (Al Jazeera) suggests possible new arrests or detentions of suspected foreign agents.

Theme 8: Domestic pressure and social cost. Confidence: almost certain that the fuel crisis, energy squeeze, and rising cost of living will remain prominent in Iranian media and social conversation. I expect at least one report of localized fuel shortages or power rationing. The Panahi sentencing will generate some international media attention and possibly a small diplomatic note, but a major domestic protest wave in the next week is unlikely unless the economic pain hits a visible breaking point.

Less likely surprises (possible but I would not build my forecast around them):
- A sudden, full-scale US-Iran war with ground elements or a carrier strike group deployment. This would require a major trigger (a downed US aircraft, a mass-casualty strike) and is maybe a 15-20 percent chance.
- Iran formally announcing NPT withdrawal or a snap nuclear test. Possible but would likely be timed to a larger political moment, not just this week. Maybe 10-15 percent.
- A surprise US-Iran direct phone call between Trump and Pezeshkian or Khamenei. Not impossible given the Vance channel, but the political optics make it a 10-15 percent shot.
- A major Houthi or Hezbollah attack on a US carrier or a Saudi oil facility that drags the whole region into a new phase. Possible but not the base case. Maybe 15 percent.

Things I would not bet on:
- A full ceasefire signed and announced within the next seven days. The conditions are too far apart, and the political timing (midterms) makes both sides want to wait for a better moment.
- Iran accepting a formal security guarantee from the US or a new arms control framework. This is a longer-term goal, not a one-week development.
- A major shift in Iran's domestic power balance (e.g., Khamenei stepping down, a new supreme leader, or a cabinet reshuffle). Nothing in the headlines points to that.
- The Strait of Hormuz being fully closed or a US naval blockade being imposed. The tactical use of mines is a pressure tool, not a full blockade.
- A US-Iran joint statement or summit meeting. The channels are back-channel (Qatar, Vance, Pakistan), not a bilateral summit.
emoji_reasons: The war between the US and Iran dominated every headline this week, with fresh strikes, threats of more strikes, the Pentagon reorganizing for a new phase, and Iran vowing retaliation without geographic limits.

The Strait of Hormuz was the stage for the most dramatic new escalation: four tankers hit by mines, limpet mines washing up on UAE beaches, a Pakistan LNG cargo attacked, and a visible shift in Iran's maritime tactics.

An extraordinary density of diplomatic activity unfolded this week, from Qatari mediators shuttling to Tehran, to the Mecca Pact bringing Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani officials to Iran, to Vance opening a direct channel, all in a desperate bid to avoid a full-scale resumption of the war.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the most visible growth is in active combat. On October 24 the picture was one of a fragile stalemate: Trump was weighing a second strike, the US was rearming the George Washington, and Iran was warning of an 'offensive' doctrine. By November 1 the stalemate had cracked open into a low-intensity exchange: the US struck fishing boats off Qeshm Island, Iran shot down a US drone over Bandar Abbas, and both sides targeted each other's air defenses and bases. The shift from 'weighing' to 'doing' is the single biggest change in the overall picture. Maritime violence in the Strait of Hormuz also grew sharply. The first photograph recorded seven vessels hit and two tankers on fire; the second records four more tankers ablaze from limpet mines, a Pakistan LNG cargo attacked with Iranian approval, oil washing up on UAE beaches, and Iran threatening legal action against South Korean Sinokor vessels. The Financial Times called this a 'tactical shift,' meaning Iran is trading big weapons for small, persistent, hard-to-attribute mines. That is a qualitative change in the character of the fighting, not just a quantitative one. Diplomacy grew in intensity and desperation. The first photograph showed shuttle visits by Pakistan's army chief and Russia's Lavrov, plus an eight-country meeting in Istanbul. The second photograph shows Qatar making repeated 'last-ditch' trips to Tehran, the so-called Mecca Pact bringing Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani officials into the same room in Tehran, and Vice President Vance reaching out to Iranian hardliners with medical supplies as a goodwill gesture. The scale of diplomatic activity is larger, but the tone is more anxious. The economic shock spread wider. The first photograph had oil at 117 dollars and the IMF warning Saudi Arabia and the UAE about recession. The second photograph adds European gas breaking above 100 euros, Canada raising interest rates, Japan scaling back fuel subsidies, ANZ raising its oil forecast, and a long list of companies from Unilever to Kia reporting rising costs. The pain is no longer a regional story; it is a global macro story. The nuclear question hardened in a concrete way. The first photograph had Iranian hardliners saying 'the time for nuclear weapons has come' and enriched uranium re-emerging as a talking point. The second photograph adds two specific developments: the IAEA reporting that Iran has not tried to repair the nuclear facilities damaged in earlier US strikes, and Iranian lawmakers formally calling for withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty. That is a step from rhetoric toward institutional positioning. Espionage and intelligence activity grew in specificity. The first photograph had two men re-arrested in the UK over RAF Fairford. The second photograph has those two men formally charged, an overseas handler identified, Russian satellites reported to have helped Iran's allies strike Saudi Arabia, a hidden network of military agencies slipping hardware past the blockade, and sanctioned jet fuel purchases disguised through Myanmar. The picture went from 'suspicion' to 'evidence and mechanism.' Domestic life in Iran deepened in pain and in cultural significance. The first photograph had soaring electronics prices and Balochistan unrest. The second photograph has a fuel crisis, natural gas running short, ordinary Iranians cutting back on essentials, and the Revolutionary Court sentencing acclaimed director Jafar Panahi to a new prison term and travel ban. The Houthi-Saudi front continued to escalate, with multiple Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia before and during the Tehran talks, and Hezbollah reportedly preparing for a new regional war with Iranian funds. A new variable appeared that was absent from the first photograph: Israel's own election, with Netanyahu campaigning on Trump's endorsement and his challenger Eisenkot accusing him of playing a 'dangerous game' with Tehran. That adds a domestic Israeli political layer to the Iran question that was not present eight days earlier. What shrank or vanished is relatively small. The specific threat of a Gulf undersea cable strike, mentioned in the first photograph as being in detailed planning, did not surface as a headline event. The mock art installation of Trump behind bars was a one-time gesture. The 'shadow tanker fleet ran out of oil' narrative evolved into the broader picture of Iran's fuel and gas crisis at home. The Balochistan unrest, noted in the first photograph, did not reappear as a distinct thread in the second. The overall sense of a 'stalemate' as a stable state gave way to an active, if limited, combat phase, and that is the most important shrinkage: the idea that both sides could hold still for the midterms proved less durable than expected.
delta.wind: Theme by theme, the expectation met reality with partial accuracy but a consistent underestimation of intensity. On the US-Iran military stalemate, the forecast said 'no full-scale new US military operation' but 'at least one limited or symbolic strike.' That was directionally right but too conservative. The reality was a sustained exchange: US strikes on Qeshm Island, an Iranian drone shootdown over Bandar Abbas, and both sides hitting each other's bases. This is more than 'limited or symbolic'; it is a low-intensity combat phase. The expectation that the US would wait for the midterms was partly overtaken by events, since strikes landed before November 3. The military build-up signal was confirmed by Hegseth firing the Pentagon's top military planner, which reads as operational planning for a new phase. On the Strait of Hormuz, the forecast of 'at least one or two more shipping incidents' was met and exceeded: four tankers on fire, a Pakistan LNG cargo hit, oil on UAE beaches. The tactical shift to limpet mines was not specifically predicted but fits the pattern. The expected 'test with a larger or more symbolic target such as a Gulf undersea cable' did not appear as a headline event, so that specific possibility did not materialize. On diplomacy, the forecast of continued shuttle activity and 'at least one more multilateral meeting' was met and surpassed. The Mecca Pact bringing Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani officials to Tehran, Qatar's 'last-ditch' mediation, and Vance's outreach to hardliners are all more intense and more multilateral than the 'Pakistan, Russia, and Turkey shuttle diplomacy' the forecast described. The expectation that Iran would make a new public proposal to appear reasonable was partly met in Pezeshkian's 'position of strength' framing and calls for regional unity, but Iran simultaneously told mediators the latest proposals were 'unacceptable,' confirming the forecast's 'no real breakthrough' call. On the economic front, the forecast of oil above 100 dollars and new sanctions was confirmed. The global spread was broader than expected: Canada raising rates, Japan cutting subsidies, ANZ revising forecasts, and a long list of consumer companies reporting cost pressure. The IMF or World Bank issuing a new specific warning was not clearly confirmed in the second photograph, so that sub-prediction is uncertain. On the Houthi-Saudi front, the forecast of 'at least one more Houthi missile or drone attack' was met with multiple attacks. Egypt's more visible diplomatic step was confirmed in the foreign minister's warning that escalation would be 'more destructive.' The forecast did not mention Hezbollah preparing for a new regional war, which is a new element. On the intelligence front, the forecast of 'another advisory or alert to Americans' and 'another arrest or incident in Europe' was confirmed and exceeded. The formal charges in the UK, the identification of the overseas handler, the Russian satellite link, and the Myanmar jet-fuel disguise are all more detailed than the forecast's general expectation. On the nuclear question, the forecast said the issue would 'remain in the background' and was 'unlikely' to see a dramatic public move on the uranium stockpile. The IAEA report that Iran is not repairing damaged facilities is a quiet but significant development, and the lawmakers' call for NPT withdrawal is more concrete than 'background.' The forecast was directionally right that no dramatic stockpile move would happen, but the institutional hardening (NPT withdrawal call) is a step further than 'background' implies. Domestically, the forecast of 'more visible public frustration' from economic pain was confirmed by the fuel crisis, gas shortage, and people cutting back on essentials. The Balochistan unrest, specifically flagged, did not reappear as a distinct thread. The Panahi sentencing is a new and significant domestic event that was not in the forecast. The expectation of 'no large-scale protest unless a triggering event' held. On the less-likely surprises: the Israel election as a new variable was not in the forecast at all, and it is arguably the most important new development. The Hegseth firing of the top planner fits the 'visible military build-up' expectation but was not specifically predicted. The $47.1 billion war cost figure making the war politically concrete in the US was not in the forecast. The Somali piracy resurfacing was not predicted. What did not come, as expected: no full ceasefire, no US ground troops, no dramatic leadership change, no complete Hormuz reopening, no coup or natural disaster. The forecast's 'things I would not bet on' list held up well. The overall pattern of error is a consistent underestimation of tempo. The forecast correctly identified the direction of every major theme but systematically described the pace as slower and the intensity as lower than reality. The stalemate was predicted to hold; it cracked. The diplomacy was predicted to be active; it became desperate. The economic pain was predicted to spread; it spread further and faster. The nuclear question was predicted to stay in the background; it moved toward the foreground with the NPT withdrawal call. The core error is treating the midterms as a firm temporal boundary when in fact both sides are acting on a compressed clock, and the military and economic pressures are not waiting for November 3 to arrive.
delta.driver: The force pushing Iran from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a political timetable and an operational reality that refuses to hold still. Trump wanted to time a major decision for after the November 3 midterms, using the war as a campaign weapon and then settling it for political credit. But the Strait of Hormuz was not going to wait: Iran's shadow fleet was running dry, its tanker attacks were shifting to a more persistent and harder-to-attribute mine strategy, and the economic shock was spreading from the Gulf to Canadian interest rates and Japanese fuel subsidies. Each day of inaction cost the US more in oil prices, in the credibility of its Gulf allies, and in the political capital of a war that was now visibly expensive at $47.1 billion. Iran, sensing that the US was politically vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms, escalated its maritime attacks and adopted a 'position of strength' narrative, betting that a more desperate US would be more willing to negotiate on Tehran's terms. The diplomatic track accelerated in parallel: Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, and even the US vice president were all moving at once, each trying to find a face-saving exit before the midterms locked in a new, more costly phase of fighting. The Israel election added a new variable that neither side had fully priced in: a Netanyahu victory would embolden a harder line, while an Eisenkot win would complicate the US-Israeli coordination on timing. Meanwhile, the nuclear hardening in Tehran, from the IAEA's observation that Iran is not repairing damaged facilities to the lawmakers' call for NPT withdrawal, reflects a calculation that the diplomatic window may be closing and that Iran should lock in its institutional position before any deal is struck. The underlying driver, then, is not a single decision or a single event but a compounding pressure: the war is too expensive to pause, too risky to ignore, and too politically entangled to resolve on a single timeline, and all the actors are moving at once in a space where the midterms are the nearest fixed point but not the only one.

judgment.reading_a:
Forecast A presents a well-organized eight-point picture of the coming week, plus a 'less likely surprises' section and a 'things I would not bet on' list. Its core judgment—that the US-Iran confrontation would stay in a managed-escalation mode with limited strikes rather than a full campaign—was broadly correct. The US did strike fishing boats off Qeshm Island, Iran shot down a US drone over Bandar Abbas and hit US bases, and the USS George Washington was rearming, all while Trump oscillated between 'wrapped up soon' and 'one or two sites.' A's call of 'probable at least one limited or symbolic strike or visible military build-up' was in the right zone, though the actual back-and-forth (US strikes, Iranian counter-strikes, drone shootdown) was slightly more active than 'one limited strike' implies.

A's Hormuz prediction of 'probable one or two shipping incidents' was directionally right but underestimated the volume: four tankers caught fire from mines, a Pakistan LNG cargo was hit with Iranian approval, and Iran threatened legal action over Sinokor vessels. A's mention of a possible 'Gulf undersea cable' test was not confirmed, but the broader idea of Iran testing US response was correct.

The diplomacy call was solid: A predicted active but fragile shuttle diplomacy, a multilateral meeting, an Iranian proposal, and no breakthrough. The actual week delivered Qatari mediators in Tehran, the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani 'Mecca Pact' meeting in Tehran, Vance's outreach with medical supplies, Pakistan's 'cautiously optimistic' posture, and Iran calling US ideas 'unacceptable.' No deal was signed. A's 'unlikely a real breakthrough deal will be signed' was exactly right.

On economics, A's 'almost certain oil above $100' was confirmed (six-month highs, European gas above €100, Canada raising rates, Japan cutting subsidies). The 'probable new sanctions' aligns with the reporting on Iran's hidden network slipping hardware past the blockade and sanctioned jet fuel disguised through Myanmar. The IMF/World Bank warning was not specifically confirmed in the headlines I can see, so that point is a mild miss.

The Houthi-Saudi escalation call was correct: multiple Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, Saudi interceptions, Egypt's foreign minister warning of 'more destructive' escalation. A's 'possible Egypt or another Arab state will take a more visible step' was confirmed by Egypt's FM statement and Saudi's defense minister traveling to Tehran.

The intelligence/espionage point was right: US intelligence warned Iran was trying harder to target Americans, two men were charged in the UK over the RAF Fairford plot, and an overseas handler was identified. A's 'possible another arrest or incident in Europe' was confirmed.

The nuclear call—unlikely a dramatic public move on enriched uranium—was roughly correct. The IAEA reported Iran had not repaired damaged facilities, and Iranian lawmakers called for NPT withdrawal, which is a rhetorical step in that direction but not the 'declaring a new enrichment level or moving material' A said was unlikely. So A's calibration was reasonable.

Domestically, A's 'probable economic pain generating frustration' was confirmed (fuel crisis, natural gas shortage, Iranians cutting essentials). The 'possible Balochistan unrest' was not specifically confirmed in the headlines. The Panahi sentencing and Tehran's rush to rebuild were domestic stories A did not specifically predict, though they fit the general 'economic pain and national endurance' frame.

A's 'less likely surprises' were well-calibrated: the Iranian missile test-firing did not appear, the surprise US/European leader visit to Tehran did not happen, and the direct Israeli strike before midterms did not occur. The 'things I would not bet on' list was entirely correct—no full ceasefire, no ground invasion, no coup, no complete Hormuz reopening.

A notable omission: neither the Israel election as a major theme nor the Vance outreach to Iranian hardliners were specifically called out. The $47.1 billion war cost figure and Hegseth firing the Pentagon's top military planner were specific events A's 'visible military build-up' and 'economic pressure' themes cover in spirit but not in detail.
